claim: Transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) can enhance vision in the healthy and diseased brain.
source: Transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) can enhance vision in the healthy and diseased brain.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The impact of multi-day tRNS on large-scale cortical networks is still unknown.
source: Yet, the impact of multi-day tRNS on large-scale cortical networks is still unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, representing a gap in the literature.

claim: Human subjects were trained for 4 consecutive days on two attention tasks while receiving tRNS over the intraparietal sulci, the middle temporal areas, or Sham stimulation.
source: We trained human subjects for 4 consecutive days on two attention tasks, while receiving tRNS over the intraparietal sulci, the middle temporal areas, or Sham stimulation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and procedure used in the study.

claim: Resting-state functional connectivity of nodes of the dorsal and ventral attention network (DVAN) was measured before and after training.
source: We measured resting-state functional connectivity of nodes of the dorsal and ventral attention network (DVAN) before and after training.
evidence: This describes a measurement procedure in the study.

claim: A strong behavioral improvement and increased connectivity within the DVAN was found after parietal stimulation only.
source: We found a strong behavioral improvement and increased connectivity within the DVAN after parietal stimulation only.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Behavioral improvement positively correlated with connectivity measures.
source: Crucially, behavioral improvement positively correlated with connectivity measures.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Changes in connectivity are a marker for the enduring effect of tRNS upon behavior.
source: We conclude changes in connectivity are a marker for the enduring effect of tRNS upon behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between connectivity and behavioral changes.

claim: tRNS has strong potential to augment cognitive capacity in healthy individuals and promote recovery in the neurological population.
source: Our results suggest that tRNS has strong potential to augment cognitive capacity in healthy individuals and promote recovery in the neurological population.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential applications based on the study's findings.

claim: Perceptual learning (PL) is crucial for clinical and aging populations that benefit from therapeutic interventions to recover and retain perceptual function.
source: Augmentation of visuoperceptual function through training, termed perceptual learning (PL), is crucial for clinical and aging populations that benefit from therapeutic interventions to recover and retain perceptual function.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of PL based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: PL is a pivotal tool for investigating neural plasticity.
source: PL is also a pivotal tool for investigating neural plasticity (Gilbert, 1994; Polat et al., 2004; Shibata et al., 2016; Deveau et al., 2014; Sterkin et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: PL has been linked to localized neural changes in sensory cortex and long-range sensory-attention network reorganization.
source: and has been linked to localized neural changes in sensory cortex and long-range sensory-attention network reorganization (Gilbert et al., 2001; Li et al., 2004; Sasaki et al., 2010; Fahle, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PL approaches have been limited in their applicability due to long and intensive training protocols.
source: Although promising, PL approaches have been limited in their applicability, due in part to the long and intensive training protocols which largely impede their use (Dosher and Lu, 2017; Das et al., 2014; Li et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2010a; Zhang et al., 2010b; Dosher and Lu, 2005).
evidence: This is a limitation of PL approaches supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cross-tasks training is a notable exception that significantly shortens learning protocols.
source: A notable exception is 'cross-tasks' training, in which learning protocols are significantly shortened by adopting a training procedure on two different tasks with the same stimuli simultaneously (Szpiro et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim about cross-tasks training is supported by citations.

claim: Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) has been proposed as a tool to facilitate cortical plasticity when coupled with behavioral training.
source: More recently, transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) has been proposed as a tool to facilitate cortical plasticity, particularly when coupled with behavioral training (Edwards et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: tRNS can modulate visual cortex excitability.
source: When delivered using a transcranial random noise protocol (tRNS), tES can modulate visual cortex excitability (Herpich et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: tRNS can promote visual functions in healthy subjects.
source: promote visual functions in healthy subjects (Fertonani et al., 2011; Pirulli et al., 2013; Tyler et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: tRNS can facilitate recovery of visual dysfunctions in disease.
source: and facilitate recovery of visual dysfunctions in disease (Campana et al., 2014; Camilleri et al., 2016; Herpich et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: PL coupled with tES can boost the effects of training by increasing the rate of learning across sessions.
source: Moreover, recent studies show PL coupled with tES can successfully boost the effects of training by increasing the rate of learning across sessions (Fertonani et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: tES is particularly effective when applied during task training.
source: particularly when applied during task training (Pirulli et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Behavioral improvements from tES persist for durations well beyond those obtained through PL training alone.
source: with the subsequent observed behavioral improvements persisting for durations well beyond those obtained through PL training alone (Cappelletti et al., 2013; Herpich et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The leading hypothesis is that tRNS has a stochastic resonance effect upon neurons.
source: The leading hypothesis derived from animal studies is that tRNS has a stochastic resonance effect upon neurons such that the injected subthreshold stimulation both resonates with ongoing task-related oscillatory activity and reduces endogenous noise, and thus, when applied at optimal levels, enhances the signal-to-noise of task-related spike firing (Antal and Herrmann, 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Polanía et al., 2018).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Focal tES of a node within a network can cause a cascade of functional changes selectively spreading within that network.
source: Consistent with the network oscillation component of resonant theory, extant studies on humans show that focal tES of a node within a network can cause a cascade of functional changes selectively spreading within that network (Nitsche and Paulus, 2000; Polanía et al., 2012; Antal et al., 2011; Krause et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to human studies.

claim: Modeling studies have shown changes in network dynamics within the directly stimulated area and across distal but connected cortical areas.
source: Modeling studies have likewise shown changes in network dynamics within the directly stimulated area and across distal but connected cortical areas (Kunze et al., 2016; Polanía et al., 2011; Sehm et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Many behavioral manifestations of neurological and psychiatric disorders are the consequence of altered brain network connectivity.
source: Given that many behavioral manifestations of neurological and psychiatric disorders are the consequence of altered brain network connectivity (Buckner et al., 2005; Fox et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The network-wide impact of tES could have wide clinical applications.
source: the network-wide impact of tES could have wide clinical applications.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications based on the network effects of tES.

claim: The study implemented a 4-day attention training protocol on two randomly interleaved PL tasks: orientation discrimination (OD) and temporal order judgments (TOJs).
source: Specifically, we implemented a 4-day attention training protocol on two randomly interleaved PL tasks: orientation discrimination (OD) and temporal order judgments (TOJs).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The target of the parietal stimulation was the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), a crucial node of spatial attention.
source: The target of the parietal stimulation was the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), a crucial node of spatial attention (Vossel et al., 2014; Battelli et al., 2017; Plow et al., 2014; Leitão et al., 2015; Battelli et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim about the IPS is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The attention network is often divided into the dorsal and the ventral attention sub-networks (DAN and VAN, or DVAN).
source: The attention network is often divided into the dorsal and the ventral attention sub-networks (DAN and VAN, or DVAN; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Fox et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the organization of the attention network supported by citations.

claim: There is continuous interplay between networks that enables the dynamic control of different attentional processes.
source: However, we are interested in the whole network due to the continuous interplay between networks, which enables the dynamic control of the different attentional processes (Vossel et al., 2014; Macaluso and Driver, 2005; Sani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The default mode network (DMN) is typically active during passive or resting conditions.
source: Moreover, to control for network-specific effects of stimulation, we also measured whether tRNS and training affected dynamics within the default mode network (DMN), typically active during passive or resting conditions (Raichle et al., 2001; Buckner and DiNicola, 2019).
evidence: This claim about the DMN is supported by citations.

claim: The human middle temporal complex (hMT+) has been directly implicated in visual temporal encoding.
source: Among the nodes of the DAN, the human middle temporal complex (hMT+) has been directly implicated in visual temporal encoding (Salvioni et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: hMT+ was included as a second stimulation site to evaluate the efficacy of tRNS on perceptual processes and to serve as an active control.
source: Thus, hMT+ was included as a second stimulation site to evaluate the efficacy of tRNS on perceptual processes, and to serve as an active control to determine if attention modulation was specific to parietal stimulation.
evidence: This describes the rationale for including hMT+ as a stimulation site.

claim: The study tested whether behavioral and neuromodulatory changes persisted 24 hr following the last training session.
source: We also sought to understand whether neural modulation following tRNS coupled with training would lead to long-lasting behavioral improvements, and we tested it 24 hr following the last training session by examining if behavioral and neuromodulatory changes persisted.
evidence: This describes a component of the experimental design.

claim: Lasting neural and behavioral change would suggest cortical plasticity that outlasts the end of stimulation.
source: Lasting neural and behavioral change would suggest cortical plasticity that outlasts the end of stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference about what lasting changes would indicate.

claim: There was no significant difference between groups prior to stimulation on the orientation task.
source: A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed no significant difference between groups prior to stimulation (F(2, 27)=0.575, p=0.569, ηp2=0.041).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was a main effect of session on OD performance, indicating that accuracy scores changed as a function of training.
source: This analysis revealed a main effect of session on OD performance (F(1, 27)=10.056, p=0.004, ηp2=0.271), indicating that accuracy scores changed as a function of training.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: There was no significant main effect of stimulation condition alone on OD performance.
source: There was no significant main effect of stimulation condition alone on performance (F(2, 27)=0.273, p=0.763, ηp2=0.020).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was a significant interaction between stimulation condition and session on OD performance.
source: Crucially, the analysis revealed a significant interaction between stimulation condition and session (F(2, 27)=11.257, p<0.001, ηp2=0.455), indicating that learning from the pre- to post-test sessions varied significantly depending on the stimulation site.
evidence: This is a key statistical finding from the study.

claim: Only the Parietal group showed significant improvement in orientation judgment accuracy between the pre- and post-test sessions.
source: We found that only the Parietal group showed significant improvement in orientation judgment accuracy between the pre- and post-test sessions (t(9)=−4.53, p=0.001, average improvement 29.8%, Cohen's d=−1.43)
evidence: This is a statistical result from pairwise comparisons.

claim: There were no significant differences between pre- and post-test performance for the hMT+ group on the OD task.
source: while there were no significant differences between pre- and post-test performance for the hMT+ group (t(9)=−0.608, p=0.558, average improvement 2.2%, Cohen's d=−0.19)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: There were no significant differences between pre- and post-test performance for the Sham group on the OD task.
source: nor for the Sham group (t(9)=0.602, p=0.562, average decrease –3.1%, Cohen's d=−0.19).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: There was a significant difference in performance improvement between Parietal and Sham conditions on the OD task.
source: Bonferroni post-hoc pairwise comparisons revealed a significant difference in performance improvement between Parietal and Sham conditions (p=0.003, Cohen's d=1.76)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: There was a significant difference in performance improvement between parietal and hMT+ on the OD task.
source: and between parietal and hMT+ (p≤0.001, Cohen's d=1.64)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: hMT+ and Sham did not differ significantly in performance improvement on the OD task.
source: while hMT+ and Sham did not differ significantly (p=1.0, Cohen's d=0.38).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: There were no significant differences between groups at baseline on the TOJ task.
source: A one-way ANOVA on pre-test session data revealed no significant differences between groups at baseline (F(2, 27)=0.14, p = 0.867; ηp2=0.010).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was no main effect of session on TOJ performance.
source: A mixed factors repeated measures ANOVA revealed no main effect of session (F(1, 27)=0.496, p=0.48; ηp2=0.018)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was no main effect of condition on TOJ performance.
source: nor of condition (F(1, 27)=0.669, p=0.521; ηp2=0.047) on performance.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was no significant interaction between session and stimulation condition on TOJ performance.
source: There was also no significant interaction between session and stimulation condition (F(2, 27)=0.589, p=0.562; ηp2=0.042), which indicates that performance in the pre- and post-test session did not differ depending on stimulation condition.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of training days on OD performance during training.
source: We found a significant main effect of training days (F(1.97, 53.31)=8.89, p<0.001; ηp2=0.248)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training data analysis.

claim: There was no main effect of stimulation condition on OD performance during training.
source: but no main effect of stimulation condition (F(2, 27)=2.9, p=0.068; ηp2=0.181).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training data analysis.

claim: There was a significant two-way interaction between stimulation and training day on OD performance.
source: Importantly, the analysis revealed a significant two-way interaction between stimulation and training day on performance (F(3.94, 53.31)=4.37, p=0.004; ηp2=0.245), indicating the effects of training on performance depended on stimulation condition.
evidence: This is a key statistical finding from the training data.

claim: tRNS administered during training caused learning that was significantly different among stimulation groups from the third day of training.
source: tRNS administered during training caused learning that was significantly different among stimulation groups from the third day of training (Training Day 3: F(2,27)=4.65, p=0.018; ηp2=0.257)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training data analysis.

claim: The difference in learning among stimulation groups remained sustained on the final day of training.
source: and remained sustained on the final day of training (Training Day 4: F(2,27)=6.63, p=0.005; ηp2=0.330).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training data analysis.

claim: The Parietal group performed significantly better than the hMT+ group on Training Day 3.
source: Post-hoc pairwise t-tests revealed the Parietal group performed significantly better than the hMT+ group on Training Day 3 (t(18)=3.6, p=0.00; Cohen's d=1.51)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: The Parietal group approached significance when compared to Sham on Training Day 3.
source: and approached significance when compared to Sham (t(18)=2.03, p=0.056, Cohen's d=0.91)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: hMT+ and Sham did not differ significantly on Training Day 3.
source: while hMT+ and Sham did not differ significantly (t(18)=0.9, p=0.37, Cohen's d=−0.40).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: On training Day 4, there was a significant difference in performance between the Parietal and the hMT+ groups.
source: Similarly, on training Day 4, we found a significant difference in performance between the Parietal and the hMT+ groups (t(18)=3.6, p=0.002; Cohen's d=1.61)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: On training Day 4, there was a significant difference in performance between Parietal and Sham.
source: and between Parietal and Sham (t(18)=3.102, p=.006); Cohen's d=1.39
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: There was no significant difference between hMT+ and Sham on training Day 4.
source: but not between hMT+ and Sham (t(18)=0.58, p=0.57; Cohen's d=−0.26).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: Parietal group performance on training Day 1 was significantly different from performance on training Day 2.
source: We found that performance on training Day 1 was significantly different from performance of training Day 2 (t(9)=−3.34, p=0.009; Cohen's d=−1.056)
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-group comparisons.

claim: Parietal group performance on training Day 1 was significantly different from performance on training Day 3.
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-group comparisons.

claim: Parietal group performance on training Day 1 was significantly different from performance on training Day 4.
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-group comparisons.

claim: Parietal group performances on the OD task significantly increased on each stimulation training session relative to the first training session.
source: These comparisons indicate that Parietal group performances on the OD task significantly increased on each stimulation training session relative to the first training session (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from statistical comparisons and illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no significant effect of training session on TOJ performance.
source: There was no significant effect of training session on TOJ performance (F(1.8, 53.50)=2.707, p=0.076; ηp2=0.091)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training data analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of stimulation condition on TOJ performance during training.
source: but there was a significant main effect of stimulation condition (F(2, 27)=4.79, p=0.017; ηp2=0.262).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training data analysis.

claim: For the mean performance during the tRNS session, the Parietal stimulation group performance was significantly better than that of the Sham group on the TOJ task.
source: For the mean performance evaluated during the tRNS session, but notable not pre- and post-training (above), the Parietal stimulation group performance was significantly better than that of the Sham group (post hoc t-test: p=0.014; Bonferroni corrected; Cohen's d=1.84)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: The Parietal stimulation group performance was not significantly different from the hMT+ group on the TOJ task during training.
source: but not the hMT+ group (post hoc t-test: p=0.256, Bonferroni corrected; Cohen's d=0.77)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: No significant difference was found between Sham and hMT+ groups on the TOJ task during training.
source: no significant difference was found also between Sham and hMT+ groups (post hoc t-test: p=0.618, Bonferroni corrected; Cohen's d=0.50).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: There was no interaction between stimulation and training session on TOJ performance.
source: We note, however, that there was no interaction between stimulation and training session on performance (F(3.96, 53.506)=2.277, p=0.073; ηp2=0.144), indicating that the tRNS did not preferentially benefit training for any stimulation group on this TOJ task (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the training data analysis.

claim: The number of censored data frames was equivalent across conditions and sessions.
source: Finally, we found no main effect of condition (F(2, 27)=0.038, p=0.963; ηp2=0.003) nor session (F(1, 27)=0.619, p=0.438; ηp2=0.007) indicating that the mean number of censored data frames was equivalent across conditions and sessions.
evidence: This is a statistical result from quality control analysis of fMRI data.

claim: FC did not differ between stimulation groups at baseline (pre-test session).
source: We compared FC prior to stimulation between groups and found no significant difference (F(2, 27)=0.300, p=0.743; ηp2=0.22), indicating that FC did not differ between stimulation groups at baseline (pre-test session).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the baseline fMRI data analysis.

claim: There was a main effect of stimulation site on FC scores within the DVAN.
source: and a main effect of stimulation site (F(2, 27)=4.064, p=0.029; ηp2=0.231), indicating that the connectivity among the DVAN nodes changed as a function of where tRNS was applied.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: The interaction between stimulation condition and session on FC scores within the DVAN was highly significant.
source: Importantly, the interaction between stimulation condition and session was found to be highly significant (F(2, 27)=11.507, p<0.001; ηp2=0.460), indicating that the change in rs-FC scores differed depending on the stimulation group (Figure 3)
evidence: This is a key statistical finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: The change in rs-FC within the DVAN was persistent the day following the last combined training and stimulation session.
source: and this change was persistent the day following the last combined training and stimulation session.
evidence: This is an inference about the temporal persistence of the FC changes.

claim: FC within the DVAN differed significantly between stimulation conditions in the post-test session.
source: One-way ANOVA analysis on post-test session revealed a significant effect of stimulation condition on FC scores (F(2, 27)=11.677, p<0.001; ηp2=0.464), which indicates that FC differs on this day between stimulation conditions (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the post-test fMRI data analysis.

claim: FC scores were significantly different in the Parietal group compared to the hMT+ group in the post-test session.
source: As depicted in Figure 3, we found that FC scores were significantly different in the Parietal group compared to the hMT+ (t(18)=3.863, p=0.002; Cohen's d=1.73)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: FC scores were significantly different in the Parietal group compared to the Sham group in the post-test session.
source: and to the Sham group (t(18)=3.64, p=0.001; Cohen's d=1.63)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: FC did not differ significantly between Sham and hMT+ groups in the post-test session.
source: while FC did not differ significantly between Sham and hMT+ groups (t(18)=0.187, p=0.854; Cohen's d=0.08).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: FC scores were significantly different between the pre- and post-test sessions in the Parietal group.
source: Pairwise t-test comparisons revealed that FC scores were significantly different between the pre- and post-test sessions in the Parietal (t(9)=−2.973, p=0.016; Cohen's d=−0.94)
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-group comparisons.

claim: FC scores were significantly different between the pre- and post-test sessions in the hMT+ group.
source: and the hMT+ groups (t(9)=−2.99, p=0.015; Cohen's d=0.95)
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-group comparisons.

claim: FC scores were not significantly different between the pre- and post-test sessions in the Sham group.
source: while they were not significantly different in the Sham group (t(9)=2.217, p=0.054; Cohen's d=0.70).
evidence: This is a statistical result from within-group comparisons.

claim: Rs-FC patterns increased within the main nodes of the DVAN after parietal stimulation only.
source: Rs-FC patterns increased within the main nodes of the DVAN after parietal stimulation only, while they decreased after hMT+ and Sham stimulation (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of the FC changes observed in the data.

claim: There was no main effect of session on FC scores when analyzing all ROI pairs within the DVAN.
source: This analysis revealed no main effect of session on FC scores (F(1, 1347)=.002, p=0.964; ηp2=0.00)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the node-by-node FC analysis.

claim: There was a main effect of stimulation group on FC scores when analyzing all ROI pairs within the DVAN.
source: but a main effect of stimulation group (F(1, 1347)=23.07, p≤0.001; ηp2=0.106).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the node-by-node FC analysis.

claim: The interaction between stimulation group and session was strongly significant when analyzing all ROI pairs within the DVAN.
source: Importantly, the interaction between stimulation group and session was found to be strongly significant (F(2, 1347)=80.206, p<0.001; ηp2=0.033), which indicates a significant difference between rs-FC scores pre- and post-test sessions, depending on the stimulation condition (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a key statistical finding from the node-by-node FC analysis.

claim: FC was significantly different among the three stimulation conditions in the post-test session when analyzing all ROI pairs.
source: This analysis revealed a strong significant effect of stimulation condition on post-test FC scores (F(2, 1286.64)=81.839, p≤0.00; ηp2=0.108), which indicates that FC was significantly different on this session among the three stimulation conditions (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the post-test node-by-node FC analysis.

claim: Connectivity was significantly increased in the Parietal group compared to the hMT+ group in the post-test session when analyzing all ROI pairs.
source: T-test comparisons on post-test FC scores revealed that connectivity was significantly increased in the Parietal group compared to the hMT+ (t(865.23) = 11.59, P =< .001, df corrected for inhomogeneity of variance; Cohen's d = .773)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: Connectivity was significantly increased in the Parietal group compared to the Sham group in the post-test session when analyzing all ROI pairs.
source: and to the Sham group (t(892.6)=10.518, p<0.001, df corrected for inhomogeneity of variance; Cohen's d=0.701).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: Post-test FC scores were not significantly different between the hMT+ and the Sham groups when analyzing all ROI pairs.
source: Post-test FC scores were not significantly different between the hMT+ and the Sham groups (t(837.68)=0.357, p=0.721, df corrected for inhomogeneity of variance; Cohen's d=0.024).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: Delta FC scores were significantly different in the Parietal group compared to the hMT+ group.
source: We run t-test comparisons on the delta FC scores between condition and we found scores were significantly different in the Parietal group compared to the hMT+ (t(890.801)=11.443, p≤0.001; Cohen's d=0.763)
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparisons of FC changes.

claim: Delta FC scores were significantly different in the Parietal group compared to the Sham group.
source: and to the Sham group (t(879.469)=10.707, p≤0.001; Cohen's d=0.714)
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparisons of FC changes.

claim: Delta FC did not differ significantly between Sham and hMT+ groups.
source: while FC did not differ significantly between Sham and hMT+ groups (t(852.124)=0.594, p=0.552; Cohen's d=0.040).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparisons of FC changes.

claim: Connections between the nodes of the DVAN changed after Parietal stimulation resulting in stronger positive correlations within the network nodes.
source: Figure 4 shows how connections between the nodes of the DVAN changed after Parietal stimulation resulting in stronger positive correlations within the network nodes
evidence: This is a description of the pattern of FC changes shown in Figure 4.

claim: Connections between the nodes after hMT+ and Sham stimulation resulted in a more negative correlation, indicating decreased connectivity.
source: while the connections between the nodes after hMT+ and Sham stimulation resulted in a more negative correlation, indicating decreased connectivity .
evidence: This is a description of the pattern of FC changes for control conditions.

claim: There was no significant main effect of stimulation condition on FC within the DMN.
source: Specifically, in the first type of connectivity analysis when the network was taken as a whole (averaged connectivity representing the network), we found no effect of stimulation by site (F(2, 27)=0.09, p=0.91)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the DMN control analysis.

claim: There was no significant main effect of session on FC within the DMN.
source: nor by session (F(1, 27)=0.58, p=0.45)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the DMN control analysis.

claim: There was no interaction between stimulation condition and session on FC within the DMN.
source: and no interaction between stimulation condition and session (F(2, 27)=0.20, p=0.81).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the DMN control analysis.

claim: There was a statistically significant interaction between the effects of network and stimulation condition factors on FC modulation scores.
source: This analysis revealed a statistically significant interaction between the effects of network and stimulation condition factors on FC modulation scores (F(2, 54)=4.97, p=0.010, ηp2=0.156)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison between DMN and DVAN.

claim: There was a significant effect of the stimulation condition factor alone on FC modulation scores.
source: as well as a significant effect of the stimulation condition factor alone (F(2, 54)=7.937, p≤0.001; ηp2=0.227).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison between DMN and DVAN.

claim: The network factor alone was not significant on FC modulation scores.
source: The network factor alone was found to be not significant (F(1, 54)=0.274, p=0.603, ηp2=0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison between DMN and DVAN.

claim: FC was modulated differently between conditions within the DVAN but not within the DMN.
source: Simple main effects analysis showed that FC was modulated differently between conditions within the DVAN (p<0.001) but not within the DMN (p=0.836)
evidence: This is a statistical result from simple main effects analysis.

claim: FC modulation was different for the Parietal condition only.
source: and that FC modulation was different for the Parietal condition only (p=0.006), while it did not differ significantly for the Sham (p=0.256) nor the hMT+ conditions (p=0.418).
evidence: This is a statistical result from simple main effects analysis.

claim: There was no effect of session on FC within the DMN when analyzing all ROI pairs.
source: We also conducted a node-by-node FC analysis (all ROIs pairs within the network as single components of the network) and found no effect of session (F(1, 1347)=2.4, p=0.116)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the node-by-node DMN analysis.

claim: There was no effect of stimulation site on FC within the DMN when analyzing all ROI pairs.
source: nor of stimulation site (F(2, 1347)=0.347, p=0.707).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the node-by-node DMN analysis.

claim: The interaction between stimulation group and session was not significant for FC within the DMN when analyzing all ROI pairs.
source: The interaction between stimulation group and session was also not significant (F(2, 1347)=0.853, p=0.426; see Appendix for further details and additional analysis).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the node-by-node DMN analysis.

claim: The lack of connectivity modulation within the DMN and the specificity of rs-FC modulation found after parietal stimulation only provide strong evidence for a selective stimulation-induced effect.
source: The lack of connectivity modulation within the DMN and the specificity rs-FC modulation found after parietal stimulation only, provide strong evidence for a selective stimulation-induced effect by our stimulation and training protocol.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison between DMN and DVAN results.

claim: Subjects that displayed a higher performance improvement also tended to show higher rs-FC within the DVAN in the post-test session (r=0.44).
source: We found subjects that displayed a higher performance improvement also tended to show higher rs-FC within the DVAN (measured as the mean of the correlations within the nodes of the DVAN) in the post-test session (r=0.44).
evidence: This is a correlation result from the brain-behavior analysis.

claim: Post-session functional connectivity scores are significantly associated with changes in behavioral scores in the final test session.
source: The linear regression model revealed a significant regression coefficient (p=0.022, R-squared=0.2) which indicates that post-session functional connectivity scores are significantly associated with changes in behavioral scores in the final test session.
evidence: This is a statistical result from linear regression analysis.

claim: Subjects with higher FC scores within the DVAN in the post-test MRI session showed a positive correlation with higher behavior improvement in the OD task achieved during training (r=0.48).
source: We found that subjects with higher FC scores within the DVAN in the post-test MRI session showed a positive correlation with higher behavior improvement in the OD task achieved during training (r=0.48).
evidence: This is a correlation result from the brain-behavior analysis.

claim: Changes in behavioral performance during training are significantly correlated with post-test session connectivity scores.
source: The regression coefficient for this relationship was significant (p=0.012, R-squared=0.23) indicating that changes in behavioral performance during training are significantly correlated with post-test session connectivity scores.
evidence: This is a statistical result from linear regression analysis.

claim: Post-test functional connectivity scores within the attention network significantly correlated with behavioral improvement measured immediately at the end of the stimulation and training protocol.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that post-test functional connectivity scores within the attention network significantly correlated with behavioral improvement measured not only immediately at the end of the stimulation and training protocol
evidence: This is a summary of the brain-behavior correlation findings.

claim: Post-test functional connectivity scores within the attention network significantly correlated with behavioral improvement measured 24 hr after the end of the stimulation protocol.
source: but also 24 hr after the end of the stimulation protocol.
evidence: This is a summary of the brain-behavior correlation findings.

claim: Bilateral tRNS over the parietal cortex during training resulted in a strong boost in performance.
source: Bilateral tRNS over the parietal cortex during training resulted in a strong boost in performance, while tRNS over hMT+ and Sham had no effect on behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of the main behavioral finding.

claim: Improvement in behavior in the parietal condition positively correlated with the increase in functional connectivity within the main nodes of the DVANs.
source: Crucially, improvement in behavior in the parietal condition positively correlated with the increase in functional connectivity within the main nodes of the DVANs
evidence: This is a summary of the brain-behavior correlation finding.

claim: Concurrent training and stimulation modulated large-scale cortical dynamics, strengthening functionally selective neural pathways.
source: indicating that concurrent training and stimulation modulated large-scale cortical dynamics, strengthening functionally selective neural pathways (Chiappini et al., 2018)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by a citation.

claim: Changes in connectivity are a potential physiological marker of enduring changes.
source: a potential physiological marker of enduring changes (Polanía et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: It might be the combination of a challenging task with concurrent brain stimulation over the relevant parietal cortical circuits that facilitated fast learning.
source: While during the Sham and hMT+ control conditions no learning was achieved, our data suggest that it might be the combination of a challenging task with concurrent brain stimulation over the relevant parietal cortical circuits that facilitated fast learning
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The combination of challenging task and brain stimulation is a paradigm amenable to promote plasticity.
source: a paradigm amenable to promote plasticity (Herpich et al., 2019; Tyler et al., 2018; Cappelletti et al., 2013; Kiyonaga et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: tRNS administered on the IPS during training promoted fast learning, with performance in the parietal group significantly diverging from the control groups by the third day of training.
source: tRNS administered on the IPS during training promoted fast learning, with performance in the parietal group significantly diverging from the control groups by the third day of training.
evidence: This is a summary of the time course findings.

claim: The Parietal tRNS group displayed a build-up and cumulative trend of the facilitation effect.
source: Notably, the Parietal tRNS group displayed a build-up and cumulative trend of the facilitation effect, as accuracy increased on each training day and retained the beneficial effect acquired in the previous session.
evidence: This is a description of the pattern of learning observed in the data.

claim: The facilitation effect was not only quantitatively different from the other groups, but also selective for one task (the OD visuospatial task).
source: This facilitation effect was not only quantitatively different from the other groups, but also selective for one task (the OD visuospatial task), within the same group of participants.
evidence: This is a summary of the task-specific effects observed.

claim: The data confirm the previously observed beneficial effect of tRNS over training.
source: These data confirm the previously observed beneficial effect of tRNS over training (Cappelletti et al., 2013; Herpich et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: tRNS's enhancing properties are mostly effective when stimulation is coupled with a relevant stimulus that maximizes the related cortical response.
source: However, they further indicate that tRNS's enhancing properties are mostly effective when stimulation is coupled with a relevant stimulus that maximizes the related cortical response, like in our OD task (Kastner and Ungerleider, 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by a citation.

claim: Learning of a visuospatial attention task was achieved within a few training sessions.
source: Taken together, these behavioral results suggest that learning of a visuospatial attention task was achieved within a few training sessions
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings.

claim: The facilitation from tRNS was long lasting, as increased performance outlasted the end of stimulation for at least 24 hr.
source: and that this facilitation was long lasting, as increased performance outlasted the end of stimulation for at least 24 hr, when the last fMRI session after the end of training was performed.
evidence: This is a summary of the temporal persistence of behavioral effects.

claim: Using a multi-session stimulation approach coupled with training promoted retention of the beneficial effect of training.
source: However, using a multi-session stimulation approach coupled with training promoted retention of the beneficial effect of training, as also shown by the results in increased rs-FC after training (Chen et al., 2015; Sarabi et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Stimulation site selection within a network is crucial to obtaining successful augmentation.
source: First, in this study, we demonstrate that stimulation site selection within a network is crucial to obtaining successful augmentation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the site-specific effects observed.

claim: Performance improved only when tRNS was delivered to the parietal cortex, and was absent in all other conditions.
source: Performance improved only when tRNS was delivered to the parietal cortex, and was absent in all other conditions, including stimulation to hMT+, often included as a node of the dorsal attention network.
evidence: This is a summary of the site-specific behavioral effects.

claim: The parietal lobes have a direct involvement in visual PL and attention processes.
source: Thus, our results indicate the parietal lobes have a direct involvement in visual PL and attention processes (Giovannelli et al., 2010; Law and Gold, 2008; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Colby and Goldberg, 1999).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by citations.

claim: tRNS effects do not spread to regions in close anatomical proximity, but rather spread within strongly functionally connected circuits.
source: Second, these results indicate that tRNS effects do not spread to regions in close anatomical proximity, but rather spread within strongly functionally connected circuits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of effects observed.

claim: Learning is facilitated when the cortical processes underlying the task are stimulated while in an aroused state derived by task performance.
source: Third, our findings support the idea that learning is facilitated when the cortical processes underlying the task are stimulated while in an aroused state derived by task performance (Wright et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: tRNS can be used to rapidly reach the optimal state for learning.
source: and indicate the possibility to use tRNS to rapidly reach this optimal state.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the mechanism of tRNS.

claim: Short but effective training sessions are an ideal condition to promote learning.
source: Importantly, our study further indicates the benefits of short but effective training sessions, an ideal condition to promote learning (Censor and Sagi, 2008; Censor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The results are consistent with previous studies that used a similar cross-task training paradigm and found behavioral improvement in only one of two tasks trained.
source: Our results are consistent with previous studies that used a similar cross-task training paradigm and found behavioral improvement in only one of two tasks trained (Szpiro et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to similar studies.

claim: Making two different perceptual judgments on the same visual stimulus may require tuning of different cortical representations.
source: One potential explanation for task selective improvement is that making two different perceptual judgments on the same visual stimulus may require tuning of different cortical representations (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Simultaneous training might induce competition between two representations, ultimately leading to the enhancement of one and inhibition of the other.
source: Simultaneous training might induce competition between these two representations, ultimately leading to the enhancement of one and inhibition of the other, as suggested in the augment Hebbian reweighting model (AHRW; Dosher et al., 2013; Dosher and Lu, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to a theoretical model.

claim: When participants trained on two randomly interleaved tasks using identical visual stimuli, improvements were observed only in the OD, suggesting the training may have changed the perceptual weighting of the orientation channels.
source: Similar to Szpiro et al.' study, when our participants trained on two randomly interleaved tasks using identical visual stimuli, improvements were observed only in the OD, suggesting the training may have changed the perceptual weighting of the orientation channels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the task-specific effects.

claim: Orientation PL was apparent with very short training sessions only when coupled with tRNS over parietal cortex.
source: In line with this hypothesis, our study showed that orientation PL was apparent with our very short training sessions only when coupled with tRNS over parietal cortex, further emphasizing the role of neuromodulation in speeding up the learning process.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: The IPS has been linked to visuospatial attention in several imaging and brain stimulation studies.
source: The IPS has been linked to visuospatial attention in several imaging and brain stimulation studies (Corbetta and Shulman, 2011; Battelli et al., 2009; Battelli et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The OD task involves the processing of visuospatial components.
source: and the OD task involves the processing of visuospatial components.
evidence: This is a statement about the cognitive demands of the task.

claim: Spatial processing was not relevant in the TOJ condition and that is typically associated to more ventral areas.
source: Spatial processing was not relevant in the TOJ condition and that is typically associated to more ventral areas (Chica et al., 2011; Agosta et al., 2017; Husain and Nachev, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The temporo parietal junction (TPJ) has been linked to temporal attention.
source: The temporo parietal junction (TPJ), at the crossroad between the ventral and the dorsal visual pathways, has been linked to temporal attention (Tyler et al., 2015: Battelli et al., 2007; Husain and Rorden, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The IPS plays a pivotal role in OD across the visual space.
source: Although this explanation is rather speculative, the selectivity of the behavioral effect along with functional connectivity results might indicate that the IPS plays a pivotal role in OD across the visual space (Capotosto et al., 2013; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The parietal lobe has been associated with selective and gating attention mechanisms.
source: Moreover, the parietal lobe has been associated with selective and gating attention mechanisms (Suzuki et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: tRNS might have facilitated gating mechanisms during learning.
source: and tRNS might have facilitated these gating mechanisms during learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: The effects driven by parietal stimulation are likely due to an effective targeting of selective task-active crucial nodes.
source: Interestingly, the analysis of the current distribution during stimulation shows that the effects driven by parietal stimulation are likely due to an effective targeting of selective task-active crucial nodes (Figure 8A and B; ).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the electric field modeling shown in Figure 8.

claim: OD and TOJ functionally activated the same task-based cortical regions at baseline.
source: With a similar pattern of distributed activity, OD and TOJ functionally activated the same task-based cortical regions at baseline (Figure 8A, details for statistical analysis are reported in the 'Task-evoked brain activity' section).
evidence: This is a finding from the task-based fMRI analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The behavioral gain was dramatically different between the two tasks despite similar functional activation.
source: However, the behavioral gain was dramatically different between the two tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of the dissociation between activation and behavior.

claim: Stimulus-evoked functional activity occurring at individual brain regions is not informative about what regions are crucial for learning.
source: This clearly shows that stimulus-evoked functional activity occurring at individual brain regions is not informative about what regions are crucial for learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dissociation between activation and learning.

claim: Regions part of the same network may flexibly interact to perform and prioritize different tasks.
source: As shown in previous studies, regions part of the same network may flexibly interact to perform and prioritize different tasks (Gratton et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Functional connectivity changes among cortical areas showed unique pattern of spontaneous response at rest, after parietal stimulation only.
source: In our data, functional connectivity changes among cortical areas showed unique pattern of spontaneous response at rest, after parietal stimulation only
evidence: This is a summary of the FC findings.

claim: tRNS might have enhanced critical changes in connectivity among distributed brain regions during learning.
source: and tRNS might have enhanced these critical changes in connectivity among distributed brain regions during learning (Cole et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Task engagement or difficulty during stimulation affects the behavioral outcome.
source: Finally, some studies have analyzed the importance of task engagement or difficulty during stimulation, and have demonstrated how these factors affect the behavioral outcome (Bortoletto et al., 2015; Hsu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Task difficulty was individually tailored and equated for difficulty across subjects ensuring subjects' engagement with the task.
source: In our study, participant engagement was challenged in two ways. First, task difficulty was individually tailored and equated for difficulty across subjects ensuring subjects' engagement with the task (Waskom et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the study supported by a citation.

claim: The experimental design randomly alternated between experimental tasks, forcing the continuous switch of attention between stimulus features.
source: Second, the experimental design randomly alternated between experimental tasks, forcing the continuous switch of attention between stimulus features
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the study.

claim: Random alternation between tasks might force a strategy that favors one task due to limited available cognitive resources.
source: might force a strategy that favors one task due to limited available cognitive resources.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the task design.

claim: Brain regions in the DVAN mediate attention mechanisms and consequently shape the analysis of visual perceptual input.
source: Brain regions in this network mediate attention mechanisms and consequently shape the analysis of visual perceptual input (Kastner and Ungerleider, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The dorsal/ventral attention network plays a pivotal role in attention functions and constitutes a large occipital-frontoparietal network that controls allocation of attention to positions and visual features in space.
source: The dorsal/ventral attention network plays a pivotal role in attention functions and constitutes a large occipital-frontoparietal network that controls allocation of attention to positions and visual features in space (Kastner and Ungerleider, 2000; for a review see Fiebelkorn and Kastner, 2020: Vossel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Tasks requiring selective attention have been shown to activate the ventral part of the attention network (VAN).
source: Tasks requiring selective attention have been shown to activate the ventral part of the attention network (VAN; Corbetta et al., 2008; Vossel et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The dorsal portion of the attention network, in particular the IPS and the FEF regions, is active during many visuospatial tasks that require spatial updating and the selection of important regions of space.
source: while the dorsal portion of the attention network, in particular the IPS and the FEF regions, is active during many visuospatial tasks that require spatial updating and the selection of important regions of space (Kastner and Ungerleider, 2000; Corbetta et al., 1998; Merriam et al., 2003; Greenberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Almost all connections between the node pairs displayed higher connectivity after multi-session parietal stimulation only.
source: Consistent with the relevance of both ventral and dorsal streams of the attention network for the performance of the task used in this experiment, our results show increased functional connectivity within the entire network. Almost all connections between the node pairs displayed higher connectivity after multi-session parietal stimulation only.
evidence: This is a summary of the FC findings.

claim: Bilateral hf-tRNS over the parietal lobes modulated the whole attention-related network, instead of producing local changes alone.
source: This result indicates that bilateral hf-tRNS over the parietal lobes modulated the whole attention-related network, instead of producing local changes alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the widespread FC changes.

claim: The neural modulation was network-specific, not a propagation of stimulation across neighboring cortical regions or networks.
source: Importantly, the neural modulation was network-specific, not a propagation of stimulation across neighboring cortical regions or networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DMN control analysis.

claim: The node-selective effect within the DVAN was demonstrated in the hMT+ stimulation group, where the neighboring IPS was not modulated by hMT+ stimulation.
source: Moreover, the node-selective effect within the DVAN was demonstrated in the hMT+ stimulation group, where the neighboring IPS was not modulated by hMT+ stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary of the site-specific FC effects.

claim: Previous physiological studies on non-human primates found changes in the lateral intraparietal area but not in the MT area suggesting that PL requires the involvement of higher areas.
source: Similar to our results, previous physiological studies on non-human primates found changes in the lateral intraparietal area but not in the MT area suggesting that PL requires the involvement of higher areas that induce changes in how the sensory information is interpreted to drive behavior (Law and Gold, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to animal studies.

claim: While hMT+ might be involved in attentional processing, for other functions involved in learning, such as decision processing, the parietal lobe plays a more pivotal role.
source: The lack of improvement in the hMT+ stimulation condition might indicate that while this cortical area might be involved in attentional processing (Yates et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2016), for other functions involved in learning, such as decision processing, the parietal lobe plays a more pivotal role (Herrington and Assad, 2010; Zhou and Freedman, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The results are consistent with previous research that found persistent network dynamics changes following other types of stimulation.
source: Our results are also consistent with previous research that found persistent network dynamics changes following other types of stimulation (e.g., transcranial magnetic stimulation, TMS; Battelli et al., 2017; Ruff et al., 2006; Ruff et al., 2008; Lee and D'Esposito, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to TMS studies.

claim: The neuromodulation protocol can be used to exert long lasting and distal effects.
source: and points to the possibility to use our neuromodulation protocol to exert long lasting and distal effects.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential applications.

claim: One potential limitation of the study is the relatively small sample size.
source: Finally, one potential limitation of our study is the relatively small sample size, given all the conditions we tested.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: Brain-behavioral correlations can produce inflated effect sizes with the combination of relatively small sample size and stringent alpha-correlations.
source: As previously pointed out, brain-behavioral correlations can produce inflated effect sizes with the combination of relatively small sample size and stringent alpha-correlations (Yarkoni, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Functional connectivity changes following parietal stimulation are likely to have affected behavior and driven the system to better respond to the demands of the attention task.
source: Functional connectivity changes following parietal stimulation are likely to have affected behavior and driven the system to better respond to the demands of the attention task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the brain-behavior relationship.

claim: Rapidly evolving changes in connectivity between interconnected regions have been proposed as the key mechanism that allows large-scale networks to respond to task demands.
source: Rapidly evolving changes in connectivity between interconnected regions have been proposed as the key mechanism that allows large-scale networks to respond to task demands (Buschman and Kastner, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: A fast modulation of the network connectivity can be due to the temporal summation of neural activity, as well as to the offline stochastic effect of tRNS.
source: In the context of tRNS, we speculate that a fast modulation of the network connectivity can be due to the temporal summation of neural activity, as well as to the offline stochastic effect of tRNS (Chaieb et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: The stochastic resonance mechanism has been proposed to lead to higher synchrony of oscillations between neurons across large-scale functional systems.
source: In fact, the stochastic resonance mechanism has been proposed to lead to higher synchrony of oscillations between neurons across large-scale functional systems, which in turn creates strong links between firing neurons (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; van der Groen et al., 2018; Schwarzkopf et al., 2011; McDonnell et al., 2009; McDonnell and Ward, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The strong correlation found between improved performance and increased FC suggests the pivotal role of the IPS in network mediating these system effects during PL.
source: The strong correlation found between improved performance and increased FC suggests the pivotal role of the IPS in network mediating these system effects during PL (Szczepanski and Kastner, 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the brain-behavior correlation supported by a citation.

claim: The modulation of task-related neural networks induced by tRNS can efficiently promote behavioral improvements and speed up the emergence of learning.
source: Our neuroimaging and behavioral results support the idea that the modulation of task-related neural networks induced by tRNS can efficiently promote behavioral improvements and speed up the emergence of learning.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: This is the first study demonstrating the sustained and selective nature by which tRNS operates on cortical dynamics.
source: Overall, this is the first study demonstrating the sustained and selective nature by which tRNS operates on cortical dynamics
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: tRNS opens a critical window during which the cortex might be more plastic and responsive to reorganization needs to promote learning.
source: and consequently opens a critical window during which the cortex might be more plastic and responsive to reorganization needs to promote learning.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the mechanism of tRNS.

claim: Clinical and healthy populations could significantly benefit from the shortened learning time afforded by the combination of tRNS with behavioral learning.
source: Clinical and healthy populations could significantly benefit from the shortened learning time afforded by the combination of tRNS with behavioral learning.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: The study was approved by the ethical committee of the University of Trento.
source: The study was approved by the ethical committee of the University of Trento.
evidence: This is a statement about regulatory approval.

claim: Thirty-seven neurologically healthy subjects participated in the study.
source: Thirty-seven neurologically healthy subjects (20 females, mean age 22.8 years old), with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in the study.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: Seven subjects were excluded from the analysis due to head motion during scanning or inadequate behavioral performance.
source: Seven subjects were excluded from the analysis due to head motion during one or both scanning procedures or due to inadequate behavioral performance (i.e., performance was at chance in catch trials), leaving 30 participants for behavioral and FC analysis.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria and final sample size.

claim: For the two active tRNS conditions, 2 mA current was applied for 25 consecutive min with random alternating frequency delivered at a high frequency range between 101 and 640 Hz.
source: For the two active tRNS conditions (Parietal and hMT+), 2 mA current was applied for 25 consecutive min with random alternating frequency delivered at a high frequency range between 101 and 640 Hz.
evidence: This describes the stimulation parameters.

claim: For Sham stimulation, the machine was turned off after the fade-in phase.
source: For Sham stimulation, the machine was turned off after the fade-in phase.
evidence: This describes the sham stimulation procedure.

claim: Participants reported no noticeable sensation resulting from tRNS.
source: Participants reported no noticeable sensation resulting from tRNS (see also Ambrus et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a report of participant experience supported by a citation.
